findings.title: New updateDevice SQL uses `?` placeholders on PostgreSQL
findings.body: The new `updateDevice` query uses `?` placeholders unconditionally (`... WHERE device_id = ? ...`), but PostgreSQL requires `$1`-style placeholders. The same file's `CreateOrUpdateDevice` explicitly uses `$1` for `migrator.Postgres`, so this path will fail when `device_limit` is reached on Postgres. Because `Anonymous.Authenticate` only treats `ErrDeviceLimitReached` as fatal and logs other TagDevice errors, a placeholder error here is swallowed and the device limit is not enforced.

findings.title: Rejected devices are cached before persistence, allowing device-limit bypass
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` checks and sets the local cache before `CreateOrUpdateDevice`. When a new device ID hits the limit, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, but the device ID is already cached. A retry with the same `X-Grafana-Device-Id` finds the cache entry, skips the device store and limit check, returns nil, and `Anonymous.Authenticate` completes successfully. This makes the configured limit trivially bypassable. Move the cache write to after a successful DB write or invalidate the key on error.

findings.title: Count-then-insert race can exceed anonymous device limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs a `CountDevices` check and then inserts when below limit without any transaction, lock, or serializable isolation. Concurrent anonymous sign-ins with different device IDs can all observe a count below `deviceLimit` and then insert, exceeding the configured limit. If the limit is intended to be enforced, the count and insert/update must be made atomic.
